title: Connect: The Intuit Story
hook: The team does not need a louder motto. It needs one target it can test.
counterintuition: Most teams assume connection means adding structure to work they already understand. Instead, it is a way to expose what they have not chosen yet. The hard part is not writing a goal. The hard part is letting the proof change the work.
tryThisNow: Write one current goal on a sticky note. Under it, add three proof lines you could check this week, then cross out any task that would not move one of them.
keyTakeaway: A goal becomes useful when it names one outcome, shows the proof of progress, and gives people a reason to change the work while there is still time.

breakdown.fastRead:
Tobin stands with a dry marker in her hand while the team keeps adding goals to the board. The list feels good because every line has a champion. It is also the first sign of drift.

Pick one outcome. Then write the proof beside it. If the proof is vague, the goal is still a wish.

A strong OKR does not make people less ambitious. It makes ambition answerable. The team can see what matters, who owns it, and whether the work is moving.

When the room gets excited, slow the room down and ask what result would prove the excitement was real.
breakdown.deepRead:
Isolde uncaps a blue marker at 4:47 p.m. and asks the robotics team what "better" means. Nobody answers at first. They all want the same trophy, but each kid is picturing a different repair, a different drive run, a different failure from last week.

That pause is the point. OKRs force a team to split desire from proof. The objective says what is worth chasing. The key results say what the world must show before the team can claim progress. The split sounds simple, but it changes the room. People stop arguing about who cares most and start looking at the same evidence.

Bruna sees the same problem in the hospital bed-control room. A morale phrase on a card cannot clear bed 18. A clear objective tied to discharge delay can. Once the screen is named, owners appear. Transport, nursing, pharmacy, and housekeeping can see where their work touches the same wait.

The move has a limit. Bad measures can make a team chase what is easy to count. Too many measures can hide the real choice in a prettier pile. Keep the proof small and close to the behavior. If a key result would not change what someone does this week, it is probably decoration.

Use the system as a weekly truth check. Name the outcome. Name the proof. Let the proof tell the team what to do next.
breakdown.fullRead:
Quincy locks the bakery door at 6:18 p.m. and stares at the loaves nobody bought. The crew worked hard all weekend. That is what makes the miss sting. The counter crew sped up the line. The bakers added variety. Delivery cut returns. Each group can point to a sensible win, and the bakery still lost the day.

That is why OKRs start with choice. A team can be full of effort and still lack a shared aim. Effort feels honest from the inside. It also hides conflict when each person is keeping a different score. The first job is to pull the score into the open.

An objective should be plain enough to repeat while tired. It names the outcome, not every task under it. A key result should be concrete enough to make a meeting uncomfortable when it is off track. It names evidence, not hope. Put the two together and the goal starts doing real work. It tells people what to ignore, what to protect, and when to change course.

Wystan proves the point beside lane three. The swimmers do not need another speech about commitment. They need to see the target before they dive. Once the splits are posted, the work changes before the coach raises her voice. The board is not there to shame anyone. It is there to make the aim shared enough that each lap can answer it.

Carys sees the same rule at 10:11 p.m. with receipts curling by the fryer. Five taped goals have made the food truck feel serious, but none of them helped during lunch. He circles ticket time, waste pounds, and repeat orders because those three checks would have changed prep before the rush. The smaller score feels less grand. It is also the first score that can steer tomorrow.

A good OKR also protects learning. If the team misses a key result, the miss is not a verdict on character. It is information about the plan. Maybe the target was too wide. Maybe the proof was too slow. Maybe three teams were working against one another without knowing it. Public proof gives the group a way to learn without turning every review into a defense of pride.

The objection is real: numbers can shrink judgment. A team can chase the count and forget the customer, patient, student, or donor. That is why the objective matters. It keeps meaning in the frame while the key results keep honesty in the frame. One without the other tilts the system. Meaning without proof becomes a speech. Proof without meaning becomes clerical work.

So keep asking two plain questions. What outcome is worth saying no for? What proof would make us change our behavior this week? If a goal cannot answer both, it is not ready to guide the work.

When the room gets excited, slow the room down and ask what result would prove the excitement was real.

examples.title: Tobin Sets the Red Marker Beside Connect

planSpec.audience: a leader facing too many attractive goals
planSpec.stakes: whether the team leaves with a shared aim or another wish list
planSpec.requiredBeat: the protagonist stops the goal pile and asks for one objective with proof tied to let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts

examples.scenario: Tobin has red marker dust on one thumb at 8:06 a.m. in the rented conference room, staring at twelve goals boxed on the whiteboard. The founders are still adding arrows. A cold paper cup leaks on the tray by her laptop. Tobin can nod, keep the room bright, and let every goal survive, or she can erase the board and ask for one launch outcome with three proof lines. Her hand hovers over the eraser.
examples.whatToDo: Erase the crowded list, name the one outcome that carries let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts, and write three proof lines the team can inspect before the next review.
examples.whyItMatters: Teams can admire a long list and still move apart. A narrow objective with visible proof turns let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts into a shared choice instead of a private hope.

examples.title: Isolde Asks for the Number Under the Slogan

planSpec.audience: a coach turning vague ambition into proof
planSpec.stakes: whether the team learns before the next match
planSpec.requiredBeat: the protagonist turns a vague phrase into an observable check for let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts

examples.scenario: Thursday, 4:47 p.m., zip ties are scattered beside the driver-station laptop when Isolde hears the captain say, "We just need to be better." The saw in the shop next door whines through the wall. Isolde taps the match log. "Better where?" he asks. "Repair speed, handoff misses, or dead time?" The students look at the floor. Isolde must decide whether to accept the mood or make them pick one number before Saturday.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for the number under the slogan. Turn the broad wish into one observable check, then agree when and where the team will look at it.
examples.whyItMatters: A slogan protects everyone from being wrong. A number makes let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts teachable because people can see the gap while they can still adjust.

examples.title: Quincy Finds Three Goals in the Flour Bin

planSpec.audience: an owner reviewing a miss without blaming the crew
planSpec.stakes: whether the next rush gets one scoreboard or three private ones
planSpec.requiredBeat: the protagonist sees that each crew had a different hidden goal and no common proof for let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts

examples.scenario: Sunday, 6:18 p.m., Quincy stands by the Hobart mixer with flour on her shoes and twelve unsold loaves cooling hard on the rack. The counter crew chased speed. The bakers chased variety. The delivery kid chased fewer returns. All three worked hard and all three were right by their own notes. Quincy writes the failed weekend on a receipt back and sees the miss: no common scoreboard for the rush.
examples.whatToDo: Run the miss backward from the evidence. Find which private goals competed, then write one shared measure before assigning new work.
examples.whyItMatters: Hard work can cancel itself when every group tracks a different win. Shared evidence makes let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts a system instead of a blame session.

examples.title: Bruna Pauses in the Bed-Control Room

planSpec.audience: a manager choosing between morale language and measurable work
planSpec.stakes: whether patients wait because nobody names the constraint
planSpec.requiredBeat: the protagonist chooses between a broad theme and a narrow objective for let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts

examples.scenario: Tuesday, 7:32 a.m., the bed-control room smells like burnt toast from the staff toaster while Bruna, operations manager, watches red delay boxes stack on the discharge screen. The huddle card in her pocket says "excellent care, every time." The night charge nurse is rubbing her eyes. Bruna is about to read the card, then sees bed 18 waiting for transport again. She has to decide whether to keep the theme or name one measurable discharge target.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the theme with the constraint in front of the team. Pick one objective, one owner, and the next check-in where proof will be read aloud.
examples.whyItMatters: Broad themes feel safe because nobody has to choose. A named constraint makes let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts concrete enough for owners, timing, and tradeoffs.

examples.title: Wystan Pins the Scoreboard by Lane Three

planSpec.audience: a coach testing whether visible proof changes behavior
planSpec.stakes: whether effort rises because everyone can see the same target
planSpec.requiredBeat: the protagonist predicts visible proof will change the work for let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts

examples.scenario: Saturday, 5:55 a.m., chlorine bites the air as Wystan tapes a hand-drawn scoreboard beside lane three. She predicts nothing will change unless the swimmers can see one target before practice starts. Two parents whisper that the board looks too plain. By 6:40, the late arrivals are checking their relay splits without being asked. Wystan must decide whether to keep the score public all month.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the scoreboard where the work happens. Let people see the target before they act, then use the next review to learn from the result.
examples.whyItMatters: Visible proof changes the work before a manager speaks. People start comparing effort to the target, which makes let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts part of the room.

examples.title: Carys Cuts the Prep List After Closing

planSpec.audience: an operator replacing wishes with proof
planSpec.stakes: whether tomorrow's service gets cleaner or only busier
planSpec.requiredBeat: the protagonist replaces a long wish list with one objective and visible measures for let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts

examples.scenario: Monday, 10:11 p.m., receipts curl by the fryer while Carys scrubs salsa from the prep table. Before, the truck had five goals taped above the sink: faster line, happier staff, better margins, cleaner prep, bigger catering. Nothing changed. After the register jammed at lunch, Carys crossed out four and wrote one objective with three checks: ticket time, waste pounds, repeat orders. The wall finally had a counter, not a wish.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the wish list to one objective. Keep only measures that would change tomorrow's behavior if they moved the wrong way.
examples.whyItMatters: Five goals give every habit a place to hide. One goal with a few checks forces let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts into daily choices the operator can actually see.

questions.prompt: A clinic director has six patient-experience projects on one slide, two nurses free to lead them, and a waiting room that has been full before noon all week. What should she do first?
choices: Pick the one outcome that matters most this quarter and name three signs of progress.
Ask every nurse to take one project so ownership is shared.
Delay the choice until the next survey arrives.
questions.explanation: The first move is choice. let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts needs one outcome clear enough for scarce people to organize around it, then proof that shows whether the choice is working.

questions.prompt: A product team writes "improve onboarding" on the planning wall, then argues for twenty minutes because support means fewer tickets, design means fewer clicks, and sales means faster demos. Which next move fits the OKR habit?
choices: Add three more onboarding ideas to the backlog.
Turn the phrase into a clear outcome and a small set of proof lines.
Ask the sales team to decide which feature is easiest to explain.
questions.explanation: A broad phrase lets everyone picture a different win. A clear outcome with proof lines makes the goal inspectable and turns the next review into learning.

questions.prompt: A school principal sees a reading plan with tutoring, posters, parent emails, and classroom games, but no score anyone will check until June. What is the main risk?
choices: Teachers may use different books in each classroom.
Parents may not notice the plan soon enough.
The team will learn too late whether the work is helping students.
questions.explanation: Late evidence is weak evidence. The point is to see drift while the plan can still change, not to admire the activity after the deadline passes.

questions.prompt: A warehouse lead posts a weekly goal on the manager-only dashboard while pickers on the floor still see last month's numbers on a stained corkboard. What is missing?
choices: A shared scoreboard close enough to guide daily choices.
A longer explanation of why the goal matters.
A private note to each shift supervisor.
questions.explanation: Visibility matters because people adjust to what they can see. A hidden score can record results, but it cannot guide the behavior that produces them.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit misses a donor target after a loud campaign, and the director wants to start the review by asking who failed to push hard enough. What should she inspect first?
choices: Whether the staff liked the campaign language.
Whether each team had the same objective and proof of progress.
Whether the target should be hidden next time.
questions.explanation: Blame arrives too late. First check whether the system gave people one shared aim and the same evidence, because scattered proof makes honest work collide.

questions.prompt: A startup closes every task in its launch tracker, celebrates with pizza, and then sees that trial users still quit before the second session. What does that show?
choices: The team probably needs more tasks next cycle.
The goal was too visible to the team.
Task completion and real progress were treated as the same thing.
questions.explanation: Tasks are not proof. A team can finish the list and still miss the outcome if the work was never tied to evidence customers or users would show.

questions.prompt: A manager wants a stretch target for a sales team, but the reps have begun padding forecasts because nobody wants to look weak on the Monday call. Which design helps most?
choices: Tie the target to honest evidence and review it often.
Use a softer phrase so nobody feels pressure.
Keep the target private until results improve.
questions.explanation: Stretch works when it stays honest. Frequent review and visible evidence keep ambition from becoming a performance of confidence instead of a way to learn.

questions.prompt: A review meeting turns sour because engineering claims uptime improved, support claims tickets fell, and marketing claims sign-ups rose, yet the customer result did not budge. What would have prevented the fight?
choices: A shorter meeting with fewer people in the room.
One shared key result that crossed the functions.
A reminder that each function owns its own lane.
questions.explanation: A shared key result gives functions one crossing point. Without it, each group can be locally right and still make the whole plan harder to steer.

questions.prompt: A leader is writing next quarter's OKR after three missed support targets and wants a draft that will guide daily choices rather than sound polished. Which draft is strongest?
choices: Make support better for customers.
Ship the support redesign and train the team.
Cut first-response time to under four hours while keeping satisfaction above 90 percent.
questions.explanation: The strongest draft names both the outcome and the evidence. It avoids a vague wish and avoids a task list that could be finished without changing the result.

reviewCards.front: A team has too many goals on the board. What do you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask which outcome deserves scarce attention now, then ask what proof would show real movement. let teams see each other's goals so help can move before the deadline hurts starts when the team chooses before it measures.

reviewCards.front: You see a goal written as a mood or slogan. What is the repair?
reviewCards.back: Translate it into an objective and a few key results. The objective keeps the meaning. The key results make the meaning answerable to visible facts.

reviewCards.front: A review meeting turns into excuses. What should you inspect?
reviewCards.back: Inspect whether the proof was close enough to the work. If the team only saw the score at the end, the measure could judge them but could not help them learn.

reviewCards.front: A stretch goal is making people perform confidence. What is the harder move?
reviewCards.back: Keep the ambition, but make misses discussable. Review evidence often, separate learning from blame, and change the plan when reality teaches something useful.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning intent into visible proof. Name one outcome, choose only a few measures, and review them often enough that the evidence can change behavior before the deadline.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work meeting lists more than three priorities, then I will ask which one result carries the week and what proof we will check by Friday.
If I set a health goal, then I will pair it with one visible measure I can check tonight, such as minutes walked, meals prepared, or bedtime.
If my personal project feels busy but stuck, then I will write the outcome in one sentence and remove tasks that do not change the proof.
If I promise someone a change, then I will name the next visible sign they can notice instead of asking them to trust my intent.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, take one active goal and rewrite it as one objective plus three proof lines. Put the proof where you will see it before doing the work.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every Friday, review one goal for ten minutes. Keep, change, or cut the key results based on what the week showed, then choose the next visible action.

memorableLines.text: If the proof is vague, the goal is still a wish.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a quick test for weak OKRs.

memorableLines.text: OKRs force a team to split desire from proof.
memorableLines.why: It names the mechanism in plain words.

memorableLines.text: Meaning without proof becomes a speech.
memorableLines.why: It warns against inspirational goals with no evidence.
